name: Sarashi / datemaki chest wrap

card.summary: Traditional Japanese cotton cloth and undersash wrapped around the chest and midsection to flatten the torso for a smooth silhouette under clothing.
card.note: Tight wraps can restrict breathing; clinicians advise against overly tight binding.

quick.overview:
Sarashi is a long strip of bleached white cotton wrapped around the chest or abdomen; the datemaki (datejime) is a wide undersash that flattens a kimono and its under-layer. Both smooth the torso so clothing hangs cleanly.

Women have also used wraps to flatten the chest for a slimmer or more androgynous outline, and the wrap is part of traditional dress, festivals and martial arts.
quick.how: The cloth is wound around the torso under clothing, and datemaki is tied over the under-kimono. Elastic or silk versions of datejime exist.
quick.risks: Breast binding in general is associated with shortness of breath, chest pain, skin irritation and rarely rib problems; guidance cited on Wikipedia advises correct sizing, not sleeping in binders and binder-free days.[3]

lead: Sarashi (bleached cloth) is a white cotton, less often linen, cloth used in Japan for garments such as the juban under-kimono, fundoshi and tenugui; a length may also be wrapped around the chest to bind the breasts, or around the body as a haramaki.[2]

The datemaki or datejime is a wide undersash that flattens and keeps in place the kimono or nagajuban, and can be made of silk, linen or elastic fabrics.[4] Wikipedia lists the datemaki and sarashi among Japanese traditional ways of flattening the chest.[3]
Grokipedia describes sarashi strips as several metres long and 30 to 40 cm wide, used in maternal care, martial arts and festivals, and by women to flatten the chest for a slimmer silhouette.[1]

chain: Smooth line under kimono or clothing
angle.text: The wrap flattens the torso so kimono and other clothes sit smoothly, and is used by some to present a flatter chest.

infobox: Cotton, linen; datejime also silk or elastic[2][4]
Japan; reported to trace to at least the Edo period[1]

paras: Sarashi is plain bleached cloth, and its name refers to sun-bleaching.[1] It is wrapped rather than sewn into a fixed garment.[1]

Beyond chest flattening, it serves as an abdominal binder in traditional maternal care, a core wrap in martial arts and a versatile underlayer, according to Grokipedia.[1] Datejime keeps the under-kimono flat and neat.[4]

No studies found of sarashi itself. Studies of chest binding report that almost everyone who binds has some physical effect, and a 2024 survey linked complications more to days per week of binding than hours per session.[3]

Breast binding is associated with breathing difficulty, chest pain, back and shoulder pain, skin irritation and rare rib fractures; guidance suggests correctly sized garments, limited wear and avoiding elastic bandages and tape.[3]
